expansion:
A is correct: this is herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO). The unilateral painful vesicular eruption over the forehead and upper lid fits varicella-zoster virus reactivation in the CN V1 (ophthalmic) dermatome. Crucially, vesicles on the tip of the nose are Hutchinson's sign, indicating nasociliary-branch involvement and a “HIGH risk of ocular complications” (L15,16, page 17). The photophobia and reduced vision are consistent with corneal involvement. The lecture specifically lists epithelial keratitis among HZO complications and gives “pseudodendritic ulcer” as a corneal manifestation (L15,16, page 17). It further distinguishes the HZO pseudodendrite as “smaller, stellate, lacks terminal buds” (L15,16, page 17), supporting the raised pseudodendritic lesions described here.

B is wrong because herpes simplex keratitis classically produces a dendritic ulcer with a “linear branching pattern with terminal buds on fluorescein staining” (L15,16, page 16), rather than the pseudodendritic lesions of HZO. The characteristic V1 vesicular rash with nose-tip involvement also points to HZO rather than HSV.

C is wrong because bacterial keratitis is described as acute pain, photophobia, blurred vision and mucopurulent discharge, with an epithelial defect, stromal infiltrate and circumcorneal injection (L15,16, page 9). Those features do not explain the dermatomal vesicular rash, Hutchinson's sign, or pseudodendrites.

D is wrong because Acanthamoeba keratitis is strongly associated with contact lens wear plus tap-water or swimming exposure, severe pain out of proportion to the signs, early perineural infiltrate and a late ring infiltrate (L15,16, page 18). None is described, whereas the rash distribution and pseudodendrites directly support HZO.
objective: Recognize herpes zoster ophthalmicus from V1 vesicles with Hutchinson's sign and pseudodendritic keratitis.
